ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
T2: Thread around a cylinder

One end of a thread is tied into a loop of length $L>2 \pi R$, and a cylinder of radius $R$ is put through the loop. The coefficient of friction between the thread and the cylinder is $\mu$. The free end of the thread is being pulled parallel to the axis of the cylinder (as shown by arrow in

<image_1>
the photo) while keeping the cylinder at rest. If the length of the loop is longer than a critical value, $L>L_{0}$, the loop can slide along the cylinder without changing its shape, otherwise the friction "locks" it into a place and increasing the pulling force would eventually just break the thread. Find this critical value $L_{0}$. The weight of the thread is to be neglected; the thread will not twist when being pulled.

It might be useful to know that

$$
2 \int \sqrt{1+x^{2}} \mathrm{~d} x=x \sqrt{1+x^{2}}+\operatorname{arcsinh} x,
$$

where $\operatorname{arcsinh} x \equiv \ln \left(x+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\right)$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, a vertical red cylinder can be seen, and a dark thin string is wound around the outer surface of the cylinder to form a loop, with a knot/intersection near the front side; one free end hangs downward along the axial direction of the cylinder, and the white arrow beside it also points downward in the vertical direction, indicating that the direction of the pulling force is parallel to the cylinder axis. Reasoning: The cylinder radius is R, and the string loop must go around the cylinder once. Orthogonally project the string loop in space onto the plane perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Orthogonal projection does not increase curve length, so the length of the projected curve does not exceed the original string loop length L. Since the string loop goes around the cylinder once, its projection must enclose the circular cross-section with radius R. Any closed curve enclosing that circular cross-section has length at least the circumference 2πR of that circle. Therefore, a string loop that can wrap around the cylinder and maintain a slidable shape must satisfy L ≥ 2πR. Conversely, when L > 2πR, one can take a loop almost equal to the circumference of the cylinder cross-section, and add an arbitrarily small axial inclination or slack to realize sliding around the cylinder; the coefficient of friction μ only affects the required pulling force and does not change this geometric critical length. So the critical value is L0 = 2πR.

T2: Thread around a cylinder

One end of a thread is tied into a loop of length $L>2\pi R$, and a cylinder of radius $R$ is put through the loop. The coefficient of friction between the thread and the cylinder is $\mu$. The free end of the thread is pulled parallel to the axis of the cylinder (as shown by the arrow in the photo) while keeping the cylinder at rest. If the length of the loop is longer than a critical value, $L>L_0$, the loop can slide along the cylinder without changing its shape; otherwise, the friction "locks" it into place and increasing the pulling force would eventually just break the thread. Find this critical value $L_0$.

It might be useful to know that

$$
2\int \sqrt{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\operatorname{arcsinh}x,
$$

where $\operatorname{arcsinh}x \equiv \ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)$.

method.method_draft: Use a topological projection argument. First read the photo as a vertical red cylinder with a dark thread loop encircling it once, and a white arrow showing the free end pulled parallel to the cylinder axis. From the text, take the cylinder radius R, loop length L, and the fact that the loop must pass around the cylinder. Orthogonally project the loop onto a plane perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Projection cannot increase length, and because the loop winds once around the cylinder, its projected curve must enclose the circular cross-section of radius R. Any such projected curve has length at least the circumference 2πR. Hence any possible sliding loop must have L≥2πR. Conversely, for any L>2πR one can make a loop arbitrarily close to the circular cross-section with a small axial slack/tilt; friction changes the pulling force/tension needed but not this geometric existence threshold. Therefore the critical value is L0=2πR.
method.CoT_raw:
图像描述：附图中可见一个竖直的红色圆柱，深色细线绕在圆柱外表面形成一个环，并在前侧附近有结点/交汇处；一段自由端沿圆柱轴向向下垂，旁边白色箭头也沿竖直方向向下，表示拉力方向平行于圆柱轴。

推理：圆柱半径为 R，线环必须绕圆柱一周。把空间中的线环正交投影到垂直于圆柱轴线的平面上。正交投影不会增加曲线长度，所以投影曲线长度不超过原线环长度 L。由于线环绕圆柱一次，其投影必须包围半径为 R 的圆形截面。任何包围该圆形截面的闭合曲线，其长度至少为该圆的周长 2πR。因此能绕住圆柱并保持可滑动形状的线环必须满足 L ≥ 2πR。反过来，当 L > 2πR 时，可以取一个几乎等于圆柱截面圆周的环，并加入任意小的轴向倾斜或松弛来实现绕柱滑动；摩擦系数 μ 只影响所需拉力，不改变这个几何临界长度。所以临界值为 L0 = 2πR。

method.method_draft: Use an unwrapped-cylinder length minimization. Read the photo as showing the thread lying on the cylindrical surface, with the pulled free end vertical/axial and the loop making one full turn around the cylinder. From the text, use radius R and fixed loop length L. Cut the cylinder along a generator and unwrap its surface into a plane with horizontal coordinate x=Rθ around the circumference and vertical coordinate z along the axis. A loop that encircles the cylinder once becomes a planar curve whose endpoints differ horizontally by 2πR after one circuit. Its length is L=∫sqrt(1+(dz/dx)^2) dx over a horizontal span 2πR, or symmetrically 2∫sqrt(1+(dz/dx)^2) dx. Since sqrt(1+(dz/dx)^2)≥1, the minimum possible length of such a wrapped loop is obtained when dz/dx=0, giving Lmin=2πR. The supplied integral can be used if one parameterizes a nonzero-slope trial/equilibrium family, but its limit as the axial slope goes to zero is still 2πR. Thus the critical length is L0=2πR; μ affects only the force distribution, not the minimum wrapped length.

推理：按题设与图像，线圈绕圆柱一周。将圆柱面沿一条母线剪开并展开成平面，取水平坐标 x=Rθ 表示绕圆周方向，竖直坐标 z 表示圆柱轴向。线圈绕圆柱一周时，在展开平面上对应一条曲线，其水平位移必须等于圆柱周长 2πR。若曲线写成 z=z(x)，其长度为 L=∫_0^{2πR} sqrt(1+(dz/dx)^2) dx。因为 sqrt(1+(dz/dx)^2) ≥ 1，所以 L ≥ ∫_0^{2πR} 1 dx = 2πR。最短情形是 dz/dx=0，即线圈在展开图中为水平线，对应圆柱上的一条圆周。给出的积分可用于计算非零斜率曲线的长度，但其最小极限仍是 2πR。摩擦系数 μ 只影响张力/摩擦分布，不改变绕圆柱一周所需的最小几何长度。因此临界长度为 L0=2πR。

Any closed curve enclosing that circular cross-section has length at least the circumference 2πR of that circle. Therefore, a string loop that can wrap around the cylinder and maintain a slidable shape must satisfy L ≥ 2πR. Conversely, when L > 2πR, one can take a loop almost equal to the circumference of the cylinder cross-section, and add an arbitrarily small axial inclination or slack to realize sliding around the cylinder; the coefficient of friction μ only affects the required pulling force and does not change this geometric critical length. So the critical value is L0 = 2πR.

T2: Thread around a cylinder

One end of a thread is tied into a loop of length $L>2\pi R$, and a cylinder of radius $R$ is put through the loop. The coefficient of friction between the thread and the cylinder is $\mu$. The free end of the thread is pulled parallel to the axis of the cylinder (as shown by the arrow in the photo) while keeping the cylinder at rest. If the length of the loop is longer than a critical value, $L>L_0$, the loop can slide along the cylinder without changing its shape; otherwise, the friction "locks" it into place and increasing the pulling force would eventually just break the thread. Find this critical value $L_0$.

It might be useful to know that

$$
2\int \sqrt{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\operatorname{arcsinh}x,
$$

where $\operatorname{arcsinh}x \equiv \ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)$.
